analysis.one_liner: Banned toxic fluids, including diesel fuel, in oil and gas fracking and put it under drinking-water law.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate committee that received it in May 2005 and never received a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the Safe Drinking Water Act so that hydraulic fracturing — the process of pumping fluids underground at high pressure to crack rock and release oil and gas — counted as underground injection, the category of activity the law already regulates. It would have banned the use of diesel fuel or any other pollutant the EPA lists as a priority pollutant in fracking fluids, and ordered the EPA to write rules making sure state programs regulated fracturing the same way. The purpose, stated in the bill's title, was to require nontoxic products in fracking.
analysis.who_benefits: People who drink from wells and aquifers near oil and gas drilling, whose water sources would gain federal protection against contamination from fracking fluids containing diesel or other toxic chemicals.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Households near drilling whose drinking water was unregulated

how_it_helps.text: It would have brought hydraulic fracturing within the Safe Drinking Water Act's definition of underground injection, the category Congress already regulates to protect drinking water sources.
It would have prohibited producers from using diesel fuel, or any material the EPA lists as a priority pollutant, in fluids injected to fracture oil and gas reservoirs.

It would have required the EPA to issue regulations and to ensure that state drinking-water programs regulated fracturing in accordance with the new rules, closing the gap left by state-by-state oversight.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas producers and their chemical suppliers, who would have had to reformulate fracking fluids, stop using diesel-based fluids, and operate under federal drinking-water rules for the first time.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas drillers and chemical suppliers

drawbacks.text: The mandate would have raised costs for producers: substituting nontoxic fluids for diesel and other priority pollutants requires reformulating the mixtures drillers use, and those costs could fall on domestic oil and gas output.

States would have lost some discretion: the bill directed the EPA to ensure state programs regulated fracturing in accordance with the new federal standard, reducing state flexibility over wells drilled within their borders.

At the time the bill was written, large-scale shale fracking was just beginning, so Congress had no comprehensive studies of fracking's effect on drinking water to weigh against the cost of regulation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — federal protection of drinking water from toxic fracking fluids — runs directly against a concentrated cost borne by drillers and chemical suppliers. The bill was narrow (it banned toxic fluids rather than shutting down fracturing), but Congress never weighed it: it received no hearing, no vote, and no debate. The objections above are the ones an honest supporter would have had to answer.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate sent the bill to the Environment and Public Works Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up; when that Congress ended in January 2007, the bill died without a vote.

narrative.text: Senator Jeffords introduced the Hydraulic Fracturing Safety Act of 2005 on May 19, 2005, with Lautenberg, Boxer, and Lieberman joining as cosponsors.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works.
The action history shows no further steps: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action. The bill died when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas producers came out ahead: fracturing remained outside the Safe Drinking Water Act, so producers and their fluid suppliers continued drilling with no federal drinking-water requirements on the fluids they injected underground.

for.name: Sen. James Jeffords
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. James Inhofe (R-OK)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill died there.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors and cosponsors were Democratic or independent senators aligned with Democrats, with no Republican cosponsors; the committee that buried it was chaired by a Republican, and the record contains no Republican support.

industries.note: The bill would have banned diesel and other priority pollutants in fracking fluids and subjected fracturing to Safe Drinking Water Act rules for the first time. The industry's interest was in keeping fracturing unregulated, which is what happened when the bill died in committee.

industries.industry: Oilfield service and fracking fluid suppliers
industries.note: Companies that supply and inject fracking fluids would have had to reformulate products to meet the nontoxic mandate. Their interest ran against the bill's drinking-water protections.

industries.industry: Public water systems and private well owners
industries.note: Sources of drinking water near drilling would have gained a federal backstop against toxic injection fluids. The bill's protections for this group never materialized.
